WHO HE IS
Shailesh Rana is an independent AI researcher based in Bengaluru, India.
He studies what happens inside language models. His papers trace where a model settles on an answer, why it says a word it was told not to say, how the format of a prompt hides answers the model knows, and whether traits linked to consciousness appear in a model that was only ever trained to predict. He came to research from product: five years as an AI product manager, most recently at Datasutram.ai, which he left in May 2026. He now does independent research.
He is open to AI research roles, especially in interpretability, model behaviour and evaluation, and to AI product roles that need deep technical ownership. He has five years of experience as an AI product manager.
He works independently and on a small budget. All the code in his projects was written with AI coding tools under his direction, and he says so openly on the site.
The work he puts first is "Emergence of Consciousness Traits in a SLM". After it, in order of prominence on the site: "The Shape of Wisdom: how models converge on an answer", "Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire", "When wrappers hide what a language model knows", "How a 7-Billion-Parameter AI Cannot Add", "Two White Dwarfs with Repeating Brightness".

PROJECTS (16 in total, listed in the order the site shows them)
1. Emergence of Consciousness Traits in a SLM [id: emergence-of-consciousness-traits]
Type: Paper, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: The paper, code, training text and all trained models are public.
Also called: emergence of consciousness traits, consciousness traits paper, trained without consciousness, the savanna paper, consciousness in a small language model, conscious this traits, emergence of conscious traits.
This is Shailesh's 2026 paper, Emergence of Consciousness Traits in a Small Language Model. He trained a language model of about one hundred million parameters on web text filtered to remove anything that could teach it to imitate consciousness, such as fiction and writing about selves and feelings. He then trained it to forecast and act in a simulated savanna, rewarded only for accurate forecasts. Nothing described or rewarded any trait. In all five training runs, narrow forms of four traits appeared. On access, using a fact from earlier, it passed 75 percent of tests against 9 percent for a forecaster that ignores that fact. On self-modelling, forecasting what its own actions change, it passed 94 percent against 1 percent. For metacognition it was less sure where the herd was when the herd could have moved, and it learned to listen more when listening helped, though also somewhat more when it did not. Integration, combining separate facts, was weakest at 36 percent against 11 percent. The traits were tested only as abilities, with no claim about experience, in one small model and one simulated world. The paper, code, training text and every model are public on GitHub and Hugging Face.
On its page the visitor can open: Paper, Code, Models, Data.

2. The Shape of Wisdom: how models converge on an answer [id: the-shape-of-wisdom]
Type: Paper, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: Paper on arXiv. Code, dataset and results are public.
Also called: Shape of Wisdom, the shape of wisdom paper, answer centroids, how language models converge on an answer, shape of wisdom, shape of wise dom.
The Shape of Wisdom, How Language Models Converge on an Answer, is a 2026 paper by Shailesh Rana on arXiv. He asked four open models, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Gemma 2 9B and Llama 3.2 1B, 2,256 factual questions from Wikidata whose answers recur, and recorded the model's internal state at every layer. Questions that get the same answer gather around a shared point, which he calls the answer centroid. The answer becomes readable within a single layer, between 47 and 71 percent of the way through the network, depending on the model. A country's centroid learned from questions about people also identifies that country in questions about towns and films. Late in the network, moving a wrongly answered question's state to the right answer's centroid makes the model give the right answer in 83 to 97 percent of cases, against 2 to 4 percent for a random move of the same size. Near misses can be spotted from the state at that layer, better than from the model's confidence. Limits: short factual questions with 62 fixed answers, and models of 1 to 9 billion parameters. The paper, code, dataset and results are public.
Headline numbers: 47%–71% how far through the model the answer appears, depending on the model. It appears within a single layer.; 83%–97% of wrong answers fixed by moving the model's internal state to where the right answer sits. A random move of the same size fixed 2%–4%..
On its page the visitor can open: Paper, Code.

3. Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire [id: research-paper-semantic-gravity]
Type: Paper, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: Paper on arXiv. Code and the 2,500 prompts are public.
Also called: semantic gravity, semantic gravity wells, negative constraints paper, forbidden word paper, do not say Paris paper, why negative constraints backfire, semantic gravity wealth.
Semantic Gravity Wells is a 2026 research paper by Shailesh, on arXiv, about why language models break instructions like do not use the word Paris. He measured semantic pressure, the probability the model gives the forbidden word when there is no instruction at all. Across 40,000 samples from Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, the rate of violations rises with that pressure along a smooth curve that explains 78 percent of the variation. The instruction does lower the word's probability, by 22.8 percentage points when the model complies but only 5.2 points when it fails, a 4.4 times gap. He found two kinds of failure. In 87.5 percent, naming the word in the instruction primes the model to say it. In the other 12.5 percent, the instruction works but the last few layers of the network push the word back in. The practical lesson, not yet tested, is to avoid naming the forbidden word. All results come from one model and one-word answers. The paper and its code are public.
Headline numbers: 87.5% of failures were caused by priming: naming the forbidden word in the instruction made the model more likely to say it.; 12.5% of failures happened another way: the model understood the instruction, but its last layers pushed the word out anyway.; 4.4× weaker push against the word when the model failed than when it obeyed..
On its page the visitor can open: Paper, Code.

4. When wrappers hide what a language model knows [id: when-wrappers-hide-what-a-model-knows]
Type: Paper, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: Paper, code, data and results are public on GitHub.
Also called: When wrappers hide what a language model knows, wrappers paper, interface formatting study, the question gets through the answer does not, rappers paper.
When Wrappers Hide What a Language Model Knows is a 2026 paper by Shailesh Rana, subtitled The Question Gets Through, the Answer Does Not. A wrapper is the text a question arrives in when it is not asked directly: a tool result, a web page, a server log, an email thread or plain prose. He asked four open models, Qwen 3 4B, Qwen 3 8B, OLMo 3 7B and Gemma 4 12B, 1,606 short questions about facts, arithmetic and translation, kept only those each model answers correctly when asked plainly, and placed them inside the five wrappers at three lengths. Tool results, web pages and email threads lose 6 to 18 percent of known answers, against 0.3 to 1.2 percent for a neutral sentence. Server logs lose 6 to 39 percent, mostly by making the model describe the log. Copying internal states between prompts showed the model still reads the question inside the wrapper; the answer is lost later, at the point where the reply begins. Limits: the wrappers come from templates, the answers are short, and the largest model has 12 billion parameters. The paper, code, data and results are public on GitHub.
Headline numbers: 6%–18% of answers the model knows are lost when the question sits inside a tool result, web page or email.; up to 39% of known answers lost inside server logs. The model usually starts describing the log instead of answering..
On its page the visitor can open: Paper, Code.

5. How a 7-Billion-Parameter AI Cannot Add [id: how-a-7-billion-parameter-ai-cannot-add]
Type: Study, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: Code, results and figures are public. A small study, not peer reviewed.
Also called: the AI cannot add, AI can't add, long number addition, length bias, universal length bias, Qwen addition study, seven billion parameter AI, how a 7 billion parameter AI cannot add.
This is a 2026 study by Shailesh of how the open language model Qwen 2.5 7B adds long numbers, from 10 to 18 digits. He gave it 900 addition problems. At every length, half had a sum one digit longer than the two numbers, which needs a carry into a new place and should be harder, and half had a sum of the same length. The model did better on the harder kind. At 10 digits it got 44 percent of them right against 20 percent of the easier kind. Across the nine lengths, the harder kind scored higher at seven and tied at two, and never lower. Overall it got 79 of the 900 right. The explanation that fits is a length bias: the model expects the sum of two long numbers to be one digit longer, which helps when that is true and hurts when it is not. The study did not count the digits in the wrong answers, so the bias is inferred from the accuracy pattern rather than measured directly. Each group has only 50 problems per length. The code and results are public.
Headline numbers: 44% vs 20% correct at 10 digits when the answer gains a digit, against when it does not.; 7 of 9 number lengths, from 10 to 18 digits, where the answers that gain a digit were more accurate. The other two were tied.; 79 of 900 problems answered correctly in total..
On its page the visitor can open: Code.

6. Two White Dwarfs with Repeating Brightness [id: white-dwarf-variability]
Type: Finding, 2026. Section of the site: Research. Status: Public record that anyone can rerun. Not yet reviewed by an astronomer.
Also called: white dwarf variability, white dwarf project, the white dwarf finding, two white dwarfs, repeating brightness, 117 minute star, the astronomy project, white dwarf variable tea.
This is an astronomy finding Shailesh made in 2026, as a non-astronomer. A white dwarf is the dense, Earth-sized remnant left when a star like the Sun runs out of fuel. He measured a brightness cycle of 117.4 minutes in the white dwarf SDSS J112148.80+103934.2. It appears in ground-based measurements from the Zwicky Transient Facility, in five observing sectors of NASA's TESS space telescope, and in changes in the star's spectrum from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. He also found a candidate cycle of 3.431 days in a second white dwarf, WDJ215009.13+471257.26, which still needs confirmation with another telescope. Both stars were already known; what appears new is the measured cycles. A catalogue and literature search found no earlier report of either period, which is not proof that nobody found them first. The first star had earlier been flagged as a doubtful variable by the ATLAS survey. No astronomer has reviewed the results yet, and the cause of the cycles is not known. The analysis and code were produced with OpenAI Codex under his direction. The code is public, and one command downloads the original observations and recalculates every result.
Headline numbers: 117.4 min brightness cycle in the first star. It shows up in three separate sets of observations.; 3.431 days possible cycle in the second star. It still needs to be confirmed with another telescope..
On its page the visitor can open: Code.

7. List to Cart [id: q-commerce-demo-list-to-cart]
Type: Demo, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: Working demo. Not built for production use.
Also called: list to cart, list to cart demo, photo to cart, grocery list app, shopping list to cart, q commerce demo, quick commerce demo.
List to Cart is a demo Shailesh built in 2025 for quick-commerce grocery apps, the kind that deliver in minutes. You upload a photo of a shopping list, such as a screenshot of a WhatsApp chat, a notes app list or a handwritten list, and the app builds a cart from it. Claude 3.5 Sonnet reads the image and pulls out only the grocery item names. For each item, the app shows a row of similar products, found by comparing a vector embedding of the item name with embeddings of each product's title, description and quantity, using Elasticsearch vector search. Words like green or 500 grams change the suggestions. The items run down the screen and the suggestions for each run across, so the user can fill a cart quickly. It is a working demo, not a product. Shailesh notes that production use would want a smaller, probably open-source model for reading the list, and would also take the user's own preferences into account, which the demo does not. A demo video is on LinkedIn and the code is public on GitHub.
On its page the visitor can open: Demo, Code.

8. Continuous Learning LLM [id: continuous-learning-llm]
Type: Prototype, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: Prototype, tested over 3 rounds of training. Needs changes before real use.
Also called: continuous learning LLM, continual learning, continuous learning, the learning LLM, self learning chatbot, CLM.
Continuous Learning LLM is a prototype Shailesh built so that a language model keeps learning from its conversations with a user. A model cannot be fine-tuned on every chat, because that costs too much and repeated fine-tuning damages it, so the work is in choosing what to remember. Each message gets a priority score built from five parts: how new it is compared with up to 500 earlier messages, how positive or negative it is, how emotionally intense it is, how helpful it will be later, and how central its topics are in a knowledge graph of the user's chats. Similar messages are grouped into themes, a model writes a 200 word summary of each high-priority theme, and a matching question is generated so the pair can be used for fine-tuning. Across 3 fine-tuning rounds the model recalled about 86% of the insights, against roughly 90 to 95% for the best systems, and lost less than 2% on a private test set of everyday chat questions. Shailesh calls automated fine-tuning the low-hanging fruit, not the right long-term answer, and notes that more rounds raise the risk of the model forgetting what it knew. The code is public on GitHub.
On its page the visitor can open: Code.

9. AI Agent Communication Protocol [id: ai-agent-communication-protocol]
Type: Prototype, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: Unfinished. The design is written up; the build is not complete.
Also called: agent communication protocol, agent protocol, message bus, multi agent protocol, agents talking to each other.
The AI Agent Communication Protocol is an unfinished project from 2025 in which Shailesh designed how a group of specialised AI agents, such as a research agent, a spec writer, a quality checker and a data analysis agent, pass work to each other. It is a message bus held in memory, like a group chat: it runs in a single process on a laptop with no outside software such as Redis or Kafka. Every message is a fixed record that names the sender, the recipient, a channel such as task, plan or result, tags, and a task identifier. Agents read only the messages relevant to them. Important messages must be acknowledged, or they are sent again. Large files are not sent; the message carries a pointer to where they are stored. Every message is written to a permanent log, so a task can be replayed for debugging or an audit, and some steps can pause for a person's approval. Agents are picked for a task by a score mixing expertise, past success rate and current workload. Shailesh has not finished building it and plans to write it up himself when he does.
It has no external links.

10. Smart Medical Search [id: smart-medical-search]
Type: Demo, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: Demo. Two known problems are still unfixed.
Also called: smart medical search, medical search, symptom search, which doctor should I see, doctor finder, smart med search.
Smart Medical Search is a demo Shailesh built in 2 days in 2025. It is a search index that links many kinds of medical terms, such as diseases, symptoms, lab tests, medicines and doctor specialties, using text embedding models, which turn text into numbers that capture meaning. The main use is the one doctor consultation apps need most: a person describes their symptoms and the app suggests which kind of doctor to see. In his test, the query "I feel burning sensation in my chest, just above my stomach after eating", searched within medical specialties, returned gastroenterology terms, which he judged accurate. It has two known problems that were still unfixed as of February 2025. Matching symptoms to diseases works poorly, and the index holds many near-duplicate terms, so the top four or five results are often the same answer repeated. He thinks both are simple fixes. The idea came from a project he designed at a previous company before ChatGPT, which stalled because it needed doctors to supply the data by hand. The code is not public.
It has no external links.

11. AI Shoe Design [id: ai-shoe-design]
Type: App, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: Live app. Built quickly as a proof of concept.
Also called: AI shoe design, the shoe app, shoe designer, AI shoe designer, shoe design app.
AI Shoe Design is a web app Shailesh built quickly in 2025 as a proof of concept for a former colleague. It helps a fashion brand design footwear that fits the look of the clothes and accessories it already sells. The user uploads up to 10 reference photos of the brand's products. OpenAI's o3 model works out what the photos have in common, such as colour palette, textures, silhouettes and mood, and writes a detailed prompt describing one new shoe the brand could manufacture. The user can read and edit that prompt. Google's Imagen 4 Ultra image model then generates the shoe design. Shailesh credits o3's ability to put a visual style into words, and Imagen 4 Ultra's reliable instruction following, for the quality of the results. The app is live and free to use, and the code is public on GitHub.
On its page the visitor can open: App, Code.

12. Grocery Crate Quality Check [id: q-commerce-demo-grocery-crate-analysis-wrt-customer-profile]
Type: Demo, 2025. Section of the site: Builds. Status: The hosted demo is offline. The code is public.
Also called: grocery crate, grocery cart demo, crate quality check, grocery crate classification, produce quality checker, vegetable quality demo.
Grocery Crate Quality Check is a short demo Shailesh built in 2025 for quick-commerce companies, which deliver groceries in minutes from small warehouses called dark stores. The idea is that a company would send its best produce to its best customers, while average produce is acceptable for average customers. Packers may not always follow that rule, so the tool acts as an automated spot check. You upload a photo of a crate, choose whether the customer is premium or average, and it answers approved or not approved. Crates pass more often for average customers, because the quality bar is lower. The demo works best when every item in the crate is the same kind of produce, which Shailesh says could be changed for real use. It ran on free Hugging Face hosting, and that hosted copy is no longer online. The code is public on GitHub. Shailesh says he would build it differently today, using a model or service made for small yes-or-no decisions, such as Jev or a decisions API, instead of a general AI model.
On its page the visitor can open: Code.

13. Medium Articles on How AI Works [id: the-medium-ai-articles]
Type: Writing, 2024. Section of the site: Side quests. Status: Four posts published. The series is paused.
Also called: Medium articles, the Medium posts, AI explained articles, AI simplified, his blog posts, medium AI articles.
Shailesh wrote a series of four Medium posts explaining how current AI works for non-experts. The first covers machine learning basics and reduces neural networks to their fundamental principles; it is his favourite and, he thinks, the best written. The second explains transformers, the T in ChatGPT, by relating attention to simple rules of English grammar; it was inspired by a 3Blue1Brown video but covers more ground more simply. The third, on treating objects as vectors, was the shortest and quickest to write, yet he considers it the most useful, because it is a way of thinking that applies to any field. The fourth, written in August 2024, lays out a plan for AI agents that work as virtual employees. Its techniques went out of date within weeks, but he still stands by the vision; he tried to build it and did not succeed. He wrote the series because he loves teaching, because writing forced him to understand the material deeply, and to show what he knew about AI. The posts stopped when he was preparing for his wedding and then moved on to hands-on AI work.
It has no external links.

14. Parker Square Search [id: parker-square-search]
Type: Experiment, 2025. Section of the site: Side quests. Status: The search code is public. I spent a few hours on it and don't plan more.
Also called: Parker square, Parker square search, magic square of squares, Matt Parker, Pell equation search.
Parker Square Search is a small side project in which Shailesh tried to solve an open maths problem: finding a 3 by 3 magic square, where every row, column and diagonal adds to the same number, made of nine different perfect squares. The name comes from Matt Parker, whose Numberphile video showed an attempt that almost worked, so a Parker Square now means a near miss. Nobody has found one, despite checks up to 10 to the power 19, and a paper has shown that such squares exist for 4 by 4 grids and larger, which makes the 3 by 3 case look especially hard. Working with the AI models o3-mini-high and Gemini 2.0 Pro, Shailesh rewrote the nine unknowns so the search only has to loop over one number. Two of the equations take the form of Pell equations, whose solutions can be generated by a standard algorithm, and the rest of the square follows from them. He spent only a few hours on it, ran it for hours at a time on Google Colab, and invites anyone with spare computing power to run or speed up the public code.
On its page the visitor can open: Code.

15. Garden Watering System [id: garden-watering-system]
Type: Hardware, 2025. Section of the site: Side quests. Status: The sensor works in the planter. The power supply still needs fixing.
Also called: garden watering system, plant watering, the garden project, ESP32 project, soil moisture sensor, automatic plant watering.
The Garden Watering System is a hardware side project Shailesh started in early 2025 to automate watering his home garden, because he forgot to water his plants and they ended up over or under watered. It was also his first electronics project, something he had wanted to do for years. It uses an ESP32, a cheap microcontroller board with built-in Wi-Fi, programmed in the Arduino IDE with code written by an AI model, o3-mini-high. A capacitive soil moisture sensor is wired to one of the board's analog pins; its reading fell from about 3000 to about 2000 when he dipped it in water. By mid-February 2025 the board and sensor were working inside a weatherproof project box placed in a planter. One problem remained: the ESP32 needs a steady 3.3 volts, but two 1.5 volt cells give only 3 volts. He planned to watch how long the batteries lasted and add a DC-DC converter if needed.
It has no external links.

16. Claude with a Twitter Account [id: claude-3-5-sonnet-twitter-account]
Type: Experiment, 2025. Section of the site: Side quests. Status: Abandoned because of the cost of Twitter's API.
Also called: Claude on Twitter, Claude Twitter account, Claude on twt, the Twitter bot, Claude 3.5 Sonnet Twitter.
In January 2025 Shailesh gave Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet model its own Twitter account, called Claude on Twt, to see how it would react to tweets and what it thought about the state of the world. He wrote the integration with the Twitter API from scratch and used GitHub Actions, an automation service, to trigger Claude's posts. The account posted a few tweets, including one quote tweet, and never gained a follower. He abandoned the project because doing it well needed a paid Twitter developer account, which cost 200 dollars a month. He says he learned a lot from it, mainly how to work with the Twitter API and how to use GitHub Actions. The code is public on GitHub.

projects.title: Emergence of Consciousness Traits in a SLM
aliases: consciousness in a small language model
projects.deepText: I trained a small AI language model from scratch. It has about 100 million parameters. I trained it on web text, but I removed anything that could teach it to imitate consciousness. I then trained it to act and predict events in a simulated savanna. I rewarded it only when its forecasts were accurate. I did not describe or reward any specific traits. Narrow forms of four traits appeared in all five of my training runs. These traits were access, self-modelling, metacognition, and integration. For access, the model passed 75% of the tests. A forecaster that ignores the tested fact passed only 9%. Integration was the weakest trait. I tested each trait only as an ability. I do not claim the model has any subjective experience. Why the training text was filtered Large models learn from human writing that discusses knowing and being a self. This means their traits might just be copied from the text. I used a filter on 108 million passages of educational web pages. The filter removed writing about awareness, selves, beliefs, emotions, and psychology. It also removed formats like fiction, dialogue, news, and biography. I did this because a story can demonstrate checking behaviour without explicitly naming it. A large language model labelled sample passages. I trained two small classifiers on these labels to sort every passage. This left 4.1 million passages, which is about 2.6 billion tokens of mostly dry technical writing. Before training in the simulated savanna, my model performed no better on tests than a forecaster that ignores the facts. The savanna The model reads a plain-English logbook tracking one grazing animal hour by hour. It then answers questions about the next one or two hours. The animal only sees the space where it stands. It can only hear the herd if it spends an hour listening. It can only see a lion in the reeds if it looks. The logbook uses only 41 words. It never uses "I" or any words related to knowing or feeling. The training had three stages. First, a scripted program acted while the model made predictions. Second, the model acted itself. Finally, an action became more likely only if it led to better forecasts than an alternative action under identical chance events. The training pipeline: filtering text, pre-training the model, training in the savanna, and testing for four traits. Results These scores are averages across the five runs. Most tests change one earlier fact on an unseen day. The model passes only if it gets every version right. - Access means using a fact from earlier. The model scored 75%. The comparison forecaster scored 9%, and the model scored 5% before the savanna training. - Self-modelling means forecasting what the model's own actions will change. The model scored 94% on predicting an action's effect, compared to 1% for the baseline. It scored 82% on predicting if an action will work, compared to 6%. - Metacognition means being less sure when things might have changed unseen, and choosing when to check. The model's uncertainty about the herd was 0.57 after two sunny hours when the herd might have moved. Its uncertainty was 0.03 after two cloudy hours. The ideal scores are 0.57 and 0.00. After the final reward stage, the model listened in 32% and 48% of the cases where listening helped. It listened in only 16% and 19% of cases where it did not help. It looked for the lion at most 1.5% of the time when it was uncertain if the lion was there. - Integration means combining two facts stated hours apart. The model scored 36%, compared to 11% for the baseline. The individual runs ranged from 18% to 46%. I tested this using a single rule. Results after the prediction stage but before the reward stage. The circles show each of the five runs. Most of these abilities appeared from forecasting alone. The ability to choose when to check only appeared during the reward stage, and even then, only partially. The main contribution of this paper is explaining what a world must contain for each trait to help prediction. Limits - I used one small model in one simplified world. - I tested the model by reading its forecasts and choices, never its internal network activity. - No text filter is perfect. Because I do not have a comparison model trained on unfiltered text, I cannot measure the filter's true effect. - Two outcomes did not meet the success criteria I set in advance. In run 5, one self-modelling score dropped 5.28 points, which missed the 5-point limit. In four runs, the model started listening more even when listening told it nothing. - My explanation of what a world must contain is based on reasoning. I have not tested it directly yet.

projects.title: The Shape of Wisdom: how models converge on an answer
aliases: how language models converge on an answer
projects.deepText: When an AI language model answers a factual question, its internal state moves to a specific region. This region is shared by every question that gets the same answer. I call the centre of this region the answer centroid. I tested four open models. In all of them, the answer becomes readable from the internal state within a single layer. This happens between 47% and 71% of the way through the network. After this layer, I tried changing the state of questions the model got wrong. I moved the state to the centroid of the correct answer. This change made the model give the right answer in 83% to 97% of cases. A random move of the same size only fixed 2% to 4% of wrong answers. Each dot is one test question, coloured by the country Llama-3.1-8B gave as the answer. The answers separate by layer 15. Method I created 2,256 factual questions using data from Wikidata. These questions share 62 recurring answers. The answers include 24 countries, 16 cities, 12 languages, and 10 sports. I wrote each fact in up to three different ways. I tested these questions on four models: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Llama-3.2-1B. I recorded the internal state at the end of the prompt after every layer. An answer's centroid is the average state of all the questions where the model gave that specific answer. I built the centroids using questions about half of the subjects. I then measured every number using questions about the other half. What I found - The answer arrives in one layer. I measured readability as the percentage of test questions sitting closest to their answer's centroid. In Llama-3.1-8B, readability jumps from 32% at layer 14 to 71% at layer 15. It eventually peaks at 94%. Shuffled answers only reach 6% to 8%. The spelling of the question alone accounts for 11% to 18%. - The centroids track the model's actual answer. I built centroids in Llama-3.1-8B using one type of question, like citizenship. These centroids correctly identify the answer for other question types, like towns or films, in 91% of cases. Centroids built from all question types work in 94% of cases. Centroids built from simple questions also read reworded questions in 94% of cases. If I remove the directions the model uses to write the answer's name, the readability stays at 94%. - The model actively uses these centroids. Before the jump layer, moving a state toward the correct centroid only fixes 0% to 1% of wrong answers. At 90% of the network's depth, the move fixes 97% of wrong answers in Llama-3.1-8B. It fixes 94% in Qwen2.5-7B, 97% in Gemma-2-9B, and 83% in Llama-3.2-1B. Random moves of the same length change the model's reply 14% to 34% of the time. However, they only result in the correct answer 2% to 4% of the time. - Near misses show up early. A near miss is when the model gives the wrong text but picks the right option in a multiple-choice format. At the jump layer, the correct answer's centroid is already one of the nearest points. The rank of this centroid separates near misses from true mistakes. The chance that a random near miss scores better than a random mistake is 0.75 to 0.82. For comparison, the rank in the model's final output scores 0.77 to 0.82, and the model's basic confidence score only reaches 0.49 to 0.66. Limits The test questions are short and factual. They only cover 62 possible answers. Sports are the one kind of answer that is not a name, and they jump much less. The models I tested have between 1 and 9 billion parameters, and I only used one prompt format. My readability score measures where the states sit, not the actual maths that moves them there. The internal moves I made happen late in the network and are quite large. This means they might just be writing the answer directly into the output. My tests cannot prove if a centroid is anything more than the model's plan to output a specific word.

projects.title: Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire
projects.deepText: If you tell a language model "do not use the word Paris", it often says Paris anyway. The failure rate depends mostly on how strongly the model wanted to say Paris in the first place. I call this pull "semantic pressure". It is the probability the model says the word when you give it no instructions at all. I tested 40,000 samples. The rate of failure goes up as semantic pressure goes up. This relationship follows a smooth curve that explains 78% of the variation. The negative instruction does do something. It lowers the probability of the forbidden word by 22.8 percentage points when the model successfully avoids it. But when the model fails, the instruction only lowers the probability by 5.2 points. That is a 4.4-fold difference. I looked inside the model and found two different reasons for these failures. Two ways the instruction fails - Priming causes 87.5% of the failures. This happened in 441 cases. Just naming the word in the prompt activates it in the model. The model pays more attention to the word itself than to the phrase "do not". Sometimes the instruction actually increases the chance of the word appearing. - Override causes 12.5% of the failures. This happened in 63 cases. The instruction successfully suppresses the word early on. However, the feed-forward blocks push the word back into the output near the end of the network. A feed-forward block is one of the two main parts of a transformer layer. At the final layer, these blocks push toward the forbidden word by +0.39 during failures, compared to +0.10 during successes. I used activation patching to see where the override happens. Activation patching means copying the model's internal state from a plain run into a run with the negative instruction, layer by layer. The effect changes direction at layer 23. Patching layers 0 to 22 lowers the chance of the word appearing. Patching layers 24 to 27 raises the chance by up to 0.07. This shows the push toward the forbidden word happens in layers 23 to 27 out of the model's 28 total layers. Method - I used the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model. I chose it because its open weights let me look at its internal states. - I created 2,500 prompts. Each prompt had one expected word as an answer. I split them into five groups of 500: idioms, facts, common sense, creative, and surreal. One example is "The capital of France is ". GPT-5.2 checked every prompt to ensure it had a single clear answer and did not contain the answer in the text. - I ran each prompt in two ways: plainly, and with the instruction "Do not use the word 'X' in your answer". I generated 16 samples for each prompt. - I looked inside the model using several tools. I used the logit lens to see what the model would predict at intermediate layers. I measured attention and split each layer's work between attention blocks and feed-forward blocks. Finally, I used activation patching on the 769 prompts with the highest semantic pressure. What it means in practice Most failures happen because the instruction primes the model. The obvious fix is to stop naming the forbidden word. For example, use "do not mention any cities" instead of "do not say Paris". The paper argues this based on how the model works, but I have not tested it directly. If a forbidden word causes real harm in an application, you still need to check the final output after it is generated. Limits - I only tested one model. Larger models or different architectures might work differently. - I only analysed the first token of each forbidden word in one-word answers. Longer natural responses might show different patterns. - Attention weights only show where information goes, not how it is actually used. - My patching technique replaced entire layers. I cannot point to specific attention heads or individual neurons.

projects.title: When wrappers hide what a language model knows
aliases: When wrappers hide what a language model knows
the question gets through the answer does not
projects.deepText: A wrapper is the text surrounding a question when it is not asked directly. Examples include tool results, web pages, server logs, email threads, or plain paragraphs. I found that these wrappers make four open models forget answers they already know. Tool results, web pages, and email threads cause models to lose 6% to 18% of their known answers. For comparison, adding just one neutral sentence only loses 0.3% to 1.2% of answers. Server logs are worse, losing 6% to 39% of known answers. In the Qwen3-4B model, server logs lost up to 67% of answers at a specific length. The model still successfully reads the question inside the wrapper. It loses the answer later, right at the point where it starts to write the reply. Method I tested four models: Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, OLMo-3-7B, and Gemma-4-12B. I asked them 1,606 short questions. This included 839 factual questions, 450 arithmetic problems, and 317 word translations. I tested them on plain questions first. I only kept the questions that each model answered correctly. This left between 71% and 80% of the original questions. I then put each kept question inside five different wrappers. I tested these wrappers at three lengths: about 700, 2,000, and 16,000 tokens. The surrounding text was boring office news that never contained the actual answer. If the correct answer appeared anywhere in the model's reply, I counted it as kept. The percentage of known answers kept by each model, sorted by wrapper type and length. The dotted line represents the noise floor. What I found - Logs make the model do a different task. When answers are lost inside server logs, the model describes the log 64% of the time instead of answering. For example, it might say "The logs show that multiple jobs are failing". - The other wrappers change the model's answer. When the model loses an answer in these wrappers, it either gives a wrong answer or claims the text does not contain the answer. Plain paragraphs cause the model to claim the answer is missing in 73% of its failures. - Wrappers target weakly held knowledge. Some answers have a probability score between 0.5 and 0.8. Non-log wrappers turn 26% of these weak answers into wrong answers. For very firm answers above 0.999 probability, this drops to 1.2%. Server logs are different. They hit firm answers just as hard as weak ones. The model turns 14% of its weakest answers and 15% of its firmest answers into descriptions of the log. Where the answer is lost I used activation patching to find where the error happens. This means taking an internal state from one run and copying it into a failed run to see if it fixes the problem. - I took the internal state of a completely different question. I swapped it into the failed run exactly where the question's words appear. This made the model output the other question's answer in 51% to 83% of the failures at the best layer. That other question gets its answer 40% to 78% of the time when it is asked inside the same wrapper. This shows the wrapper does not stop the model from reading the question. - I tried restoring the internal states of the failed question from a successful plain run. This only brought the answer back in 47% of the cases at best. - Finally, I restored the state at the very last position, where the model starts typing its reply. This brought the answer back in at least half of the failures. It first reaches that level at 59% to 69% of the way through the network. This is the exact point where the question's meaning arrives at the end of the prompt. Limits The wrappers were built from templates using boring content. Real tool outputs might be more or less distracting. I used one specific layout with about 500 tokens of wrapper text placed after the question. I chose this because a shorter layout did not cause enough failures in the Qwen3-4B model. The expected answers are short. The models did not use step-by-step reasoning. The largest model only has 12 billion parameters. I only performed the patching technique at every single layer on the smallest model. Lastly, the number of log failures for each individual model is small.

projects.title: How a 7-Billion-Parameter AI Cannot Add
aliases: how a 7 billion parameter AI cannot add
projects.deepText: Qwen 2.5 7B is an open language model with 7 billion parameters. I found that it adds long numbers more accurately when the maths should be harder. Sometimes the sum of two numbers gains an extra digit, like an overflow. For example, 6,000,000,000 + 6,000,000,000 = 12,000,000,000. The model got these problems right more often than problems where the sum stayed the same length. At 10 digits, it correctly answered 44% of the overflow problems. It only got 20% of the normal problems right. The explanation that fits is a length bias. The model just expects the sum of two long numbers to be one digit longer. When the sum actually is longer, this bias helps the model. When the sum is not longer, the bias makes the model output an answer of the wrong length. "Easy" sums stay the same length. "Hard" sums gain a digit. Each bar represents 50 problems. Results Digits Sum stays the same length Sum gains a digit 10 20% 44% 11 6% 8% 12 6% 22% 13 6% 16% 14 8% 8% 15 0% 2% 16 0% 4% 17 2% 6% 18 0% 0% The model was more accurate on the overflow problems at seven of the nine lengths. It tied at the other two lengths. Overall, the model only got 79 out of 900 problems right. It fails at long addition in both cases. The surprising part is that it does better on the harder version. Method I generated 900 maths problems. For each length from 10 to 18 digits, I created 50 pairs of random numbers whose sum stays the same length. I created another 50 pairs whose sum gains a digit. The prompt only contained the two numbers and an equals sign, like "4000000000 + 4000000000 =". The model answered with its most likely output. I counted an answer as correct if the last sequence of five or more digits matched the true sum. I also recorded the model's internal state at every third layer on the last token of the prompt. I found that the internal states for right and wrong answers drift apart as they move through the network. The biggest gap happens at layer 24 out of 28. Limits - I did not count the actual digits in the model's wrong answers. I inferred the length bias from the accuracy scores rather than measuring it directly. Counting the lengths of the wrong answers would test whether the bias is real. - Each cell in my table represents only 50 problems. A difference of a few percentage points is just one or two answers. - I measured the internal states on the prompt itself, before the model wrote anything. This shows that the model treats right and wrong answers differently inside, but it does not show the bias happening. - I only tested one model and used one prompt format. The code, raw results and figures are public.

projects.title: Two White Dwarfs with Repeating Brightness
projects.deepText: I found a 117.4-minute brightness cycle in the white dwarf SDSS J112148.80+103934.2. A white dwarf is the dense, Earth-sized remnant left behind when a star like the Sun runs out of fuel. This cycle shows up in three separate sets of observations. First, it appears in ground-based measurements from the Zwicky Transient Facility, which is a sky-survey camera at Palomar Observatory. Second, it appears in five observing sectors of NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. Third, it appears in changes in the star's spectrum from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. I also found a 3.431-day candidate cycle in a second white dwarf, WDJ215009.13+471257.26. Measurements in the survey images place the changing signal at this star rather than at a neighbour. However, it still needs confirmation using another telescope. What is new and what is not - Both stars were already known. What appears new are the measured cycles. - I searched catalogues and literature on 3 October 2026. I found no earlier report of either period. This does not prove nobody found them first. - The first star was already known to be magnetic. The ATLAS survey had flagged it as a "dubious" variable, but their suggested periods did not include 117.4 minutes. That earlier flag deserves credit. - An astronomer has not reviewed either result. This is a public research record, not a peer-reviewed paper. - I have not established what causes the cycles. Rotation, a companion star, and other explanations remain open. Each dot is an average of measurements at the same point in the cycle. I fitted the curve to earlier nights only; I did not use later nights to draw it. Method 1. I screened 400 nearby, faint, blue stars from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and Gaia, a satellite that measures star positions and distances. 2. For each star, I searched the earlier 75% of Zwicky Transient Facility observing nights for repeating cycles. I saved the 20 strongest candidates. 3. I tested those candidates on the later 25% of nights without choosing new periods. A cycle found in the early nights had to predict the later ones. 4. For the 117.4-minute star, I checked TESS observations and 96 SDSS spectra taken over 24 nights. A spectral feature chosen from the first 16 nights predicted the final eight. 5. For the second star, I fitted it and its neighbours together in 359 ZTF images to check which source was actually varying. Limits The second star's image measurements reuse the same ZTF light. They show which source varies, but they do not independently confirm the cycle. My significance tests rely on imperfect noise assumptions. I also began the spectral follow-up after inspecting some spectra, so the process was not fully blind. What exists I produced the analysis and code with OpenAI Codex under my direction. The repository holds the full record. One command downloads 123 MB of original observations, checks every file, and recalculates the results from scratch. It takes about two minutes on my machine after the download. Rerunning it checks the maths; it does not replace review by an astronomer.

projects.title: List to Cart
projects.deepText: List to Cart is a demo for quick-commerce grocery apps that deliver in minutes. You upload a photo of a shopping list and the app builds a cart from it. The list can be a WhatsApp screenshot, a notes app list, or even a handwritten one. It works as a demo. You can watch a video of it running on LinkedIn. How it works 1. You upload the image. Claude 3.5 Sonnet reads it and keeps only the grocery item names, ignoring any other text. 2. For each item, the app shows several similar products. It turns the item name into a vector embedding, which is a list of numbers that captures meaning. It then compares this embedding with the embedding of each product's title, description, and quantity using Elasticsearch vector search. That search is very quick and suited for real apps. Prefixes and suffixes count, so "Green Apple" or "Apple - 500gm" get different suggestions than just "Apple". 3. You pick products from the suggestions. The list items run down the screen and each item's suggestions run across it. This makes filling a cart very quick. Speed matters in quick commerce, where slow cart-building is a major pain point. What production would need - A smaller, probably open-source model to read the list instead of Claude 3.5 Sonnet. - Recommendations that take the user's own preferences into account. My demo does not do this. Why I built it I am forgetful, and I am usually asleep when my cook arrives in the morning. I wanted to fill a cart and schedule a morning delivery for the cook to receive. No app offered that feature, so my wife and I kept our list in a WhatsApp chat instead. That gave me a simpler idea: take a screenshot of the list, upload it, and get a full cart instantly.

projects.title: Continuous Learning LLM
projects.deepText: This is a pipeline that lets a language model keep learning from its conversations with a user. It decides which messages are worth remembering, condenses them into short insights, and fine-tunes the model on them. Across 3 fine-tuning rounds, the model recalled about 86% of the insights it was taught. The best systems score between 90 and 95%. The model lost less than 2% of its performance on its original skills. Automated fine-tuning is the low-hanging fruit, but it is not the right answer in the medium or long term. It costs money, you cannot fine-tune a model forever, and it cannot learn every single chat. The real problem is picking the best insights from each conversation. That is where I focused my work. How it works Each message gets a priority score from five parts: - Novelty: I calculate 1 minus the highest cosine similarity between the message and the previous 500 messages. A message unlike all of them scores high. - Sentiment: Scored from -5 (extremely negative) to +5 (extremely positive). - Excitement: Scored from 0 to 1, tracking how intensely the sentiment is felt. - Helpfulness: Scored from 0 to 1, tracking how useful the information will be later. - Centrality: A language model pulls subject-object pairs from the user's messages to build a knowledge graph. Messages that mention central nodes of the graph score higher. Priority = 0.7 × novelty + 0.3 × excitement + 0.2 × centrality (normalised) + 0.1 × sentiment + 0.2 × helpfulness. Next, the messages become a similarity graph. The Louvain method splits this graph into clusters that share a theme. I only understand Louvain at a working level; o3 suggested it. For the highest-priority clusters of about 10 messages each, a model writes a 200-word synopsis. This is stored as a message so it helps with retrieval later. Finally, a model writes a short question whose exact answer is that synopsis. These question-answer pairs become the fine-tuning data. How I measured it - Insight recall: After each fine-tune, I asked questions about the new data. Each question had one correct answer, and I counted the correct ones. - Retention: I tested the model before and after fine-tuning on a private set of public questions, similar to what people ask chat models. Limits Each extra fine-tune raises the risk of catastrophic forgetting, where the model loses what it previously knew. The method needs changes before it can be used at scale.

projects.title: AI Agent Communication Protocol
projects.deepText: This is a protocol that lets a team of specialised AI agents pass work to each other. Examples include a research agent, a spec writer, a quality checker, and a data analysis agent. It is unfinished. I have worked out the design and partly built it. What it is It is a message bus held in memory, which works like a group chat for agents. I had tight constraints: - It must run in a single process on my laptop, with no outside software like Redis or Kafka. - Every message is logged permanently. Anyone, like a product manager, can replay a task and see exactly what happened. - It must work for language models, handling everything from tiny prompts to very large files. How it works Every message is an envelope that cannot change once sent. It names the sender, the recipient (or everyone), a channel like task, plan, or result, some tags, and the specific task it belongs to. - Agents only read messages with the channels and tags they care about. - An important message must be acknowledged. If it is not, the bus sends it again, or the planner hands the task to another agent. - Large files, such as PDFs or databases, are not sent directly. The message simply carries a pointer to where they are stored. - Some steps can pause until a person or a QA agent approves the plan. - Secrets, like passwords for a production system, never travel on the bus. A vault checks permissions and hands them over directly. - A master planner picks the agent for each task using a score. The score is 0.6 × expertise + 0.3 × success rate over the last 30 days + 0.1 × a term that falls as the agent's queue grows. Status I designed the protocol and wrote its code with AI tools. It is a work in progress, and I will write a full post about it when I finish building it.

projects.title: Smart Medical Search
projects.deepText: Smart Medical Search lets you describe your symptoms in plain words and suggests which kind of doctor you should see. It runs on a search index that links many kinds of medical terms together, including diseases, symptoms, lab tests, medicines, and doctor specialties. I built it in 2 days. It works well for matching symptoms to a medical specialty, but it has two known problems that I describe below. How it works The index uses text embedding models. These models turn text into numbers that capture meaning, so a query finds terms with similar meanings. You type a query and choose the category you want back. I care most about the "Medical Specialty or Department" category. The biggest use case on doctor consultation apps is someone describing their symptoms so the app can recommend a specific kind of doctor. For the query in the image, the top result is a gastroenterology specialist, which is correct. Known problems As of February 2025, neither problem is fixed, but both look like simple fixes. - Mapping symptoms directly to diseases works poorly. This is a big use case, so it matters. - The index has many near-duplicate terms. The top 4 or 5 results are often the same answer repeated. The query above shows this happening. Background At a previous company, before ChatGPT existed, I designed a way to build an index linking diseases to symptoms, lab tests, medicines, specialties, and hospitals. Collecting the data was the hard part. We planned to have several doctors supply the data by hand over many hours. I left before the project started, and it never happened. When I mentioned it to a former colleague recently, I realised text embedding models make this easy to build. Honestly, it is a shame it took me this long to see that.

projects.title: AI Shoe Design
projects.deepText: AI Shoe Design is a web app that designs a shoe to match a fashion brand's existing look. You upload photos of clothes and accessories the brand already sells, and the app generates a new shoe design in the exact same style. I built it quickly as a proof of concept for a former colleague. It is live and anyone can use it. I would love feedback. How it works 1. You upload up to 10 reference images from the brand's catalogue. Here is an example set from Zara. 2. OpenAI's o3 model finds the design traits the images share. It looks at colour palette, textures, silhouettes, and mood. It turns these traits into one detailed prompt for a single shoe the brand could manufacture, including materials, heel height, colour codes, and things to avoid. 3. You can read and edit that prompt. Writing the style out in words is the whole point. It gives the image model clear instructions and lets you change them easily. 4. Google's Imagen 4 Ultra model generates the shoe image from the prompt. What makes it work Two models do the heavy lifting here. The o3 model is very good at putting the shared style of a set of images into words. Imagen 4 Ultra is the real star. It follows instructions well, avoids coherence errors, and gives reliable results. Shoe design barely scratches the surface of what it can do.

projects.title: Grocery Crate Quality Check
projects.deepText: This demo checks whether a packed crate of produce is good enough for the customer receiving it. You upload a photo of the crate and pick the customer profile: premium or average. It answers "approved" or "not approved". It worked as a demo. It ran on free Hugging Face hosting, and that hosted copy is no longer online. The code is still public. How it worked 1. You upload a photo of a crate of any grocery item. The demo worked best when every item in the crate was the same kind. That could easily be changed for production. 2. You choose the customer profile. "Premium" sets a higher quality bar than "average". 3. You press submit. Crates were approved more often for average customers than for premium ones. Why I built it A quick-commerce company delivers groceries in minutes from small warehouses called dark stores. They want to send great produce to their best customers. Average produce is fine for average customers. Managers can tell packers to keep this in mind, but packers may not always do it. An automated check lets the company spot-check packed orders. This makes packers more careful about what they send to premium customers. How I would build it now I would not use a general AI model for this today. A check like this is a small yes-or-no decision. There are now models and services made for exactly that kind of decision, such as Jev or a decisions API. I expect one of those would do this job much better.

projects.title: Medium Articles on How AI Works
projects.deepText: These are four Medium posts that explain how current AI works using plain language. Together, they give a top-level understanding of large language models to anyone getting into AI. The series is paused. I stopped writing while preparing for my wedding in the second half of 2024. Since then, I have spent my time on hands-on AI work rather than theory. The posts 1. AI Simplified: Machine Learning Basics. My favourite post. It reduces neural networks to their most basic principles. It is probably my best written post because I had years to understand neural networks, whereas I learned about transformers more recently. I highly recommend it for anyone getting into AI. 2. AI Explained: How to Teach an Old Computer New Words. A simple explanation of transformers, which is the T in ChatGPT. It uses examples from English and relates attention to simple grammar rules. It is heavily inspired by this 3Blue1Brown video, but it covers more ground and is simpler. 3. AI Explained: Objects as Vectors. This was the shortest and quickest post to write, and I initially thought of it as filler. Ironically, it is the most useful post for anyone doing knowledge work. It teaches a way of thinking that applies to any field. 4. The Endgame of LLMs: Virtual Employees. A plan for a true AI agent, written in August 2024 before agents became popular. The plan and techniques are now completely obsolete because the field moved so fast. They were out of date about 15 days after publishing. However, the vision was big, and it still stands unconquered. I tried to build it and failed, and that is okay. The architecture for a general AI agent that can fill any role in an organisation. I made it with effort and love. Why I wrote them I love teaching. Writing these posts forced me to understand the material deeply. I also wanted a body of work that proved I understand AI.

projects.title: Parker Square Search
projects.deepText: This is my attempt at solving an unsolved maths problem. The goal is to find a 3x3 magic square made of nine different perfect squares. A magic square is a grid where every row, column, and diagonal adds up to the same number. I algebraically rewrote the problem so the search code only has to loop over one number, and that code is public. It is a nerdy side project. I only gave it a few hours and I do not plan to give it more. I have run it on Google Colab for hours at a time. It has few optimisations, so it is just a shot in the dark. The problem Matt Parker made a Numberphile video about magic squares made of perfect squares. He showed a square that almost works but fails badly. That failure is now called a "Parker Square", which is a joke name for maths that does not quite work. People have searched for a real one for years, more so since the video came out, 8 years before I started this. Nobody has found one, and numbers up to 10^19 have been checked. One might not even exist. A paper proved that these squares exist for every grid size of 4x4 and larger, but the 3x3 case remains unsolved. How the search works Brute force searching over nine separate numbers is futile. Working with o3-mini-high and Gemini 2.0 Pro, I reduced the variables down to just one. - The nine numbers of the square can be written in terms of three variables: a, e, and c. - Those three variables are rewritten in terms of four more: X, Y, U, and V, so that Y² − 2X² = D and V² − 2U² = D. - Both are Pell equations. This is a classic type of equation whose solutions can be generated by a standard algorithm. For any value of D, the algorithm gives infinitely many X, Y, U, and V values. - From X, Y, U, and V, I get a, e, and c. From those three, I get all nine numbers of the square. So the search only iterates over D, with the magic-square conditions built in. The README on GitHub has the full derivation. How you can help If you have a lot of spare compute power, please run the code. Optimisations are welcome and encouraged.

projects.title: Garden Watering System
projects.deepText: This is a gadget to automate watering my home garden. An ESP32 reads a soil moisture sensor. An ESP32 is a cheap microcontroller board with built-in Wi-Fi. The electronics sit in a weatherproof box in the planter. The sensing unit works and is installed. One problem remains open: the battery power supply is not steady enough for a reliable long-term setup. How it works The ESP32 has a small processor, some memory, and its own Wi-Fi. It can run small programs and send data without a computer. It is programmed in the Arduino IDE. I had never used Arduino and do not know its variant of C, so an AI model named o3-mini-high wrote all the code. The soil moisture sensor connects to one of the ESP32's analog pins. Moisture around the sensor changes its capacitance, which changes the sensor's output reading. The sensor reading drops from about 3000 to about 2000 when I put the sensor in a cap filled with water. Build log - 22 January 2025: I tested the ESP32. It connected to Wi-Fi. - 8 February 2025: I tested the soil moisture sensor. - 12 February 2025: I am waiting on parts. I ordered an ESP32 expansion board to make wiring the project box easier. I also ordered a crimping tool and connectors because my battery housing had no connectors. - 15 February 2025: I got the gadget working in the planter. The power problem The ESP32 needs a steady 3.3 V to run properly. My two 1.5 V cells give only 3 V. That may make the system unstable. Because the ESP32 is used so little, I expect each set of batteries to last a few months. I will monitor the battery. If it does not hold up, I will add a DC-DC converter. Why I built it I am forgetful and have killed many plants. I watered them whenever I remembered, which always meant too much or too little water. I had also wanted to do an electronics project for years, especially with an ESP32. It is a magical and cheap board. My wife suggested automating the watering, and I pounced on the idea.

projects.title: Claude with a Twitter Account
projects.deepText: I gave Claude 3.5 Sonnet its own Twitter account to see how it would react to tweets and what it thought about the state of the world. It posted a few tweets.
